description: Our idea: software that tracks crew health signals (heart rate, sleep, stress), detects anomalies early, and sends clear alerts to crew and mission control, built for limited bandwidth, delayed comms, and secure data. Looking for developers, data/ML people, UI/UX designers, someone into human factors, and a storyteller or video editor. All levels welcome!
summary: HealthLoop is onboard health monitoring software for astronauts on long missions, such as a Mars round trip. Earth can be 3 to 22 light-minutes away and the link can drop out, so HealthLoop makes every health decision on the spacecraft first. It learns each astronaut's own normal for heart rate, recovery (heart rate variability), blood oxygen, stress and sleep, separately for sleep and waking hours, and flags only changes that last. The astronaut immediately sees a plain-language explanation and clear next steps, without waiting for Earth. HealthLoop then sends a tiny encrypted summary to Mission Control, where the flight surgeon sees each crew member's status with its true data age and can acknowledge alerts. Every signal is tied to a NASA Human Research Program risk and one of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. An onboard AI assistant, which runs locally because there is no internet in deep space, answers crew questions using only their own data. This matters because on long missions, astronauts must spot and act on changes in their own health.
details:
What it does

HealthLoop watches five health signals for each crew member: heart rate, recovery (heart rate variability), blood oxygen, stress and sleep. It also takes a daily check-in on fatigue, mood and symptoms. It decides on board whether something has changed, tells the astronaut in plain language what it means and what to do, and keeps Mission Control informed over a slow, unreliable deep-space link.

How it works

1. Personal baselines. HealthLoop learns each astronaut's own normal from their last two weeks, with separate baselines for sleep and waking hours. A heart rate of 52 is normal asleep but unusual awake, and one astronaut's normal can be another's warning sign.

2. Detection that avoids false alarms. Each reading is compared with that person's baseline. A single odd reading (often a loose sensor) is ignored; three unusual readings in a row (30 minutes) raise a "Watch" or "Act now". Hard safety limits, such as blood oxygen at or below 92%, alert immediately. Unusual readings are never learned into the baseline, so it cannot drift toward the problem.

3. Onboard first. Every alert shows the astronaut a plain-language explanation and concrete next steps right away. Earth is informed, but the crew never has to wait for it.

4. A realistic link to Earth. Alerts are packed into 12-byte records and routine data into 7 bytes per person, then encrypted with AES-GCM, which also detects tampering. Alerts jump the queue; if bandwidth runs short, old routine data is dropped first and alerts never are. The link applies NASA's published 3 to 22 minute Earth-Mars delay, stores and forwards everything during a communications blackout, and the flight surgeon's acknowledgements travel back with the same delay. A 30-minute update for four crew is about 64 bytes, compared with about 500 bytes as JSON.

5. An AI assistant kept in its lane. The tested detection code decides every alert. A language model only explains and summarises: it answers crew questions ("Can I exercise today?") using only that astronaut's live readings, turns free-text check-ins ("barely slept, headache since lunch") into a few bytes of structured data so the raw text never leaves the ship, and writes the flight surgeon's shift handover. On the ship it runs locally (Meta's Llama 3.2 through Ollama) because there is no internet in deep space; on Earth it can use the Claude API. Every answer is checked before use, and built-in rules take over if the model is unavailable.

Built on NASA research

We used NASA's Human System Risks and 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight to decide what to monitor. Heart rate and recovery map to the Cardiovascular Adaptations risk (gravity fields); blood oxygen to the Hypoxia risk (hostile/closed environments); stress and mood to the Behavioral Health risk and sleep to the Sleep Loss risk (isolation and confinement); and onboard-first alerts address the Earth Independent Operations risk (distance from Earth). Every alert carries its NASA risk tag.

Benefits and intended impact

Astronauts get early, personal, understandable warnings and can act immediately. Flight surgeons see the whole crew at a glance with honest data ages, using a fraction of the bandwidth. The design also suits other remote, isolated settings such as Antarctic stations, submarines and rural care.

Results

On a real ECG recording (MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, record 208), HealthLoop raised one alert during the burst of irregular heartbeats and cleared it afterwards. In a simulated week with four crew it raised no false alarms, and every injected fault (raised heart rate, low oxygen, isolation stress, sleep loss) was caught. 28 automated tests cover detection, the link, encryption, the AI features and the API.

Tools and languages

Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, FastAPI, cryptography, pytest), HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Web Crypto API, canvas), Ollama with Llama 3.2, and the Claude API. The dashboard runs on its own in any browser or on top of the Python server. Parts of the code and documentation were written with an AI coding assistant, as disclosed in the repository.

What makes it creative

A personal baseline instead of one-size-fits-all limits; an alert system that works with no Earth contact at all; a link model that shows the real cost of distance; and a calm, plain-language crew screen next to a technical Mission Control screen, because an astronaut and a doctor need different things.

Factors we considered

False alarms and alert fatigue, bandwidth and light-time delay, communication blackouts, privacy (free text stays on board), security (encryption and tamper detection), safety (the AI never decides an alert), and clarity for non-medical crew.

Limits and next steps

This is a prototype with simulated crew data, not a medical device. Next steps: connect real wearables, add a radiation dosimeter feed (radiation is the one NASA hazard we do not monitor yet), and have flight surgeons validate the thresholds.
